kurz: How capital can be converted into regular income, what a lifelong income annuity costs, how it compares with a withdrawal plan and why a combination with a later Social Security start usually performs best.

bloecke.md:
In the accumulation phase, the goal can be measured, namely as much capital as possible on the target date. In the payout phase, the money has to last as long as your life, and nobody knows how long that will be. According to US life tables, a 65-year-old has on average roughly 18 to 21 more years ahead, women more than men. This average is of little use for your own planning, because half of all cases lie above it. The difference between a retirement of 13 years and one of 33 years is the difference between a comfortable old age and a destitute one.

There are three solutions to this risk: an insurance contract that takes it over, a withdrawal plan that ignores it, and a combination of the two that splits it. In the US, there is a fourth building block that every worker already owns: Social Security, an inflation-indexed lifetime annuity whose amount you can increase by claiming later.

## Single premium immediate annuity

The single premium immediate annuity (SPIA), also called an income annuity, is an insurance contract bought with one payment and without an accumulation phase. You pay in capital once and receive an income for life, starting within a year, usually the following month. Its price is reflected in the **payout rate**, the guaranteed annual income as a percentage of the premium, or in the monthly income per $100,000. Only this figure allows two offers for the same age, sex and options to be compared.

Three quantities determine the payout. The first is the **interest rate** at which the insurer can invest the premium, mostly in bonds. Unlike in some other countries, US insurers do not price income annuities with a low regulatory maximum rate but with market rates, so payouts rise and fall with bond yields. The second is the **mortality** of annuity buyers, who live longer on average than the general population, partly because it is mainly people who feel healthy who buy annuities. The third is the insurer's costs and profit margin. Because these factors differ between insurers, quotes for the same person can differ noticeably.

bloecke.formel: Monthly income = premium ÷ 100,000 × monthly income per $100,000
bloecke.erklaerung: The quote per $100,000 combines interest rate, mortality and costs in a single figure. Once the contract is signed, the income is fixed for life; it no longer depends on how interest rates and life expectancy develop.

bloecke.md:
In this model, $100,000 becomes around $631 of guaranteed monthly income, a payout rate of about 7.6% a year. That is more than a fixed-term plan to age 95 at the same interest rate pays. The difference is the **mortality credit**: the capital of buyers who die early stays in the pool and pays for the income of those who live long. Every buyer gives up the chance of leaving the capital to heirs and receives in return a higher income that cannot run out.

The figures are a model, not a quote. Real payouts depend on the current interest rate level, age, sex, state and insurer. A higher interest rate raises the payout, a later start raises it considerably, and options such as a guarantee period lower it. For a real decision, you need current quotes from several insurers.

An income annuity is only as secure as the insurer that pays it. If an insurer fails, the state life and health insurance guaranty association steps in, but only up to limits set by state law. Many states protect at least $250,000 in present value of annuity benefits per person and insurer; some go higher, and the details differ. Anyone who wants to annuitize more than this limit can split the amount across several insurers. Financial strength ratings help in the choice; the guaranty association is the safety net, not a reason to pick the weakest insurer with the highest payout.

After purchase, an income annuity can usually not be surrendered. Most states provide a short free-look period after delivery of the contract; after that, the decision is final.

## Withdrawal plan

A withdrawal plan, by contrast, is a fixed-term payout. Capital and interest are spread over a fixed number of years, after which the account is empty. The result can be calculated to the cent. The capital remains your property, it can be inherited and is available at any time, and there are no costs for an insurance contract.

In the US, such a plan can be built from Treasury securities. A ladder of Treasury notes and bonds, or of Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS), that mature one after the other provides a known amount every year; the interest on Treasuries is exempt from state income tax. Setting it up takes some effort, and the ladder ends on a fixed date. If you live beyond it, the plan no longer pays. An income annuity, by contrast, continues without any action on your part, even at an age at which decisions about money become harder.

bloecke.md:
## Break-even age of the income annuity

The obvious break-even calculation presents the annuity in too favorable a light. Dividing $100,000 by an annual income of $7,574 gives 13.2 years; at 78 you would therefore have got back the money paid in. However, this calculation assumes that the money would earn no interest in the alternative. A comparison with a safe account earning interest from which exactly the same amount is withdrawn is more informative.

The assumptions are $100,000 in Treasury securities yielding 4.5% and an annual withdrawal of $7,574, equal to the model income.

- The account sustains this withdrawal for 20.1 years, that is, up to about age 85.
- After that, the account is empty, while the annuity keeps paying for as long as you live.
- In the model mortality, about half of the 65-year-old buyers are still alive at 85, and around 15% at 95.

The income annuity therefore pays off for those who live longer than average. That is its purpose. It is insurance against the event that you yourself are one of the long-lived, and not an investment. Because of the insurer's costs, it does not pay off in terms of expected value; it pays off in the case for which it was bought.

Measured by expected value, an income annuity costs a little; measured by the worst case, it is cheap. Anyone who buys one pays for the certainty that the income will still be paid at 97, not for a return.

## Taxes

An income annuity bought with money that has already been taxed (nonqualified) is taxed with the **exclusion ratio** under 26 U.S.C. § 72(b). The premium divided by the expected return gives the tax-free share of every payment; the expected return is calculated with the IRS life expectancy multiples in Publication 939. With a multiple of 20.0 for a 65-year-old, the expected return of $7,574 a year is $151,480, so 66% of every payment is tax-free and $2,574 a year is taxable. At a marginal tax rate of 12%, this results in around $309 of tax, that is, 4.1% of the income. Once the premium has been recovered after about 20 years, the payments become fully taxable.

An income annuity bought inside an IRA or 401(k) (qualified) is fully taxable, because the money was never taxed. Since 2014, a qualifying longevity annuity contract (QLAC) can be bought with IRA or 401(k) money up to an inflation-adjusted limit ($210,000 in 2025); its income can start as late as age 85, and the amount is excluded from the RMD calculation until then. The taxable portion of an annuity counts towards the income that determines the taxation of Social Security and Medicare surcharges.

bloecke.md: With a fixed-term plan, only the interest portion is taxable, and when fund shares are sold from a taxable account, only the gain portion. In the 12% bracket, long-term gains usually fall into the 0% band. A withdrawal from a traditional IRA, by contrast, is fully taxable regardless of the form of payout. The tax burden in retirement is therefore determined more by the type of account than by the choice between annuity and withdrawal plan.

## Splitting according to basic needs

The decision is how much capital goes into an income annuity and how much stays in the portfolio. A sound split is based on expenses, not on assets. The unavoidable monthly expenses for housing, utilities, insurance, food and transportation should be covered by income guaranteed for life. For all other expenses, income may fluctuate.

Basic needs amount to $3,600 a month, including the premiums for Medigap and Part D. Social Security at 67 pays $2,665.80; after the Part B premium of $202.90, $2,462.90 remains, and without other substantial income no federal tax is due on it.

- The gap in basic needs is $1,137 a month. Because about 4% of each payment of a nonqualified annuity goes to tax, the annuity must amount to around $1,185.
- At the model income of $631 per $100,000, this results in a capital requirement of 1,185 ÷ 631 × 100,000 = around $188,000.
- With assets of $400,000, around $188,000 is therefore annuitized, and $212,000 remains in the portfolio for travel, dental work, the car, the grandchildren and long-term care that may become necessary.

Here, just under half of the assets would be annuitized. Anyone who pays everything into the annuity gives up all flexibility for a degree of security that they only partly need.

bloecke.titel: The cheapest annuity: claiming Social Security later
bloecke.md: Before buying a private annuity, check whether delaying Social Security is cheaper. In the example, claiming at 70 instead of 67 costs 36 monthly payments of $2,665.80, that is, $95,969, and raises the benefit by 24%, or $639.79 a month for life, adjusted for inflation every year. A nominal income annuity of the same starting amount would cost around $88,000 at 70 in the model, but it would not rise with prices; an inflation-linked one would cost considerably more. For married couples, there is an additional effect: when the first spouse dies, the survivor keeps the higher of the two benefits. Delaying the claim of the higher earner therefore also raises the survivor's income. The three years until 70 are bridged from the portfolio.

## Inflation and the purchasing power of the annuity

The greatest weakness of the income annuity is less its price than its nominally fixed amount. An income of $631 is still $631 after 25 years. Social Security, by contrast, rises every January with the cost-of-living adjustment, by 2.8% for 2026. Most private income annuities have no such mechanism. Annuities with a fixed annual increase of, say, 2% or 3% exist, but they start with a considerably lower payment, and annuities linked to the consumer price index are hard to find in the US market.

bloecke.titel: Purchasing power of a nominally fixed income of $631
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation, x-axis in years from the start of payments; at 2% inflation, 55% of purchasing power is retained after 30 years, at 3% only 41%.

bloecke.md: The part of the assets that was not annuitized provides more effective protection against inflation, as does a later Social Security start. That is why the combination of the building blocks is more than a compromise. Social Security and the annuity secure basic needs, and the portfolio offsets rising prices.

The payout rises markedly with the age at purchase, because the expected remaining lifetime becomes shorter. In the model, $100,000 buys around $631 a month at 65, $727 at 70, $863 at 75 and $1,060 at 80. When annuitizing in tranches, only part of the capital is annuitized at 65, and a further tranche is bought at 75 or 80. Until then, the capital remains invested, and the later income is bought at a higher payout rate, although at the interest rates of that time.

A deferred income annuity, or a QLAC inside an IRA, achieves something similar with a single decision: you pay today for an income that starts at 80 or 85. In practice, this means annuitizing at retirement only as much as basic needs less Social Security require. The second decision is deliberately postponed to an age at which you know your own state of health and your actual spending. When comparing offers, the only thing that counts is the guaranteed income for the same premium, the same age and the same options.

bloecke.titel: Guarantee period, refund and joint life
bloecke.md: Three options reduce the loss that arises in the event of early death. With a **period certain**, payments continue to the beneficiaries after death until the end of the agreed period. A **cash refund** or **installment refund** pays out the part of the premium not yet received. A **joint and survivor** annuity pays for as long as either spouse lives. All three lower the payout; in the model, a 10-year period certain reduces it from $631 to $606. The refund options remove part of the balancing between early and late deaths on which the entire calculation is based. Wealth can be passed on more cheaply through the non-annuitized part of the portfolio than through an option in the annuity.

The SECURE Act of 2019 made it easier for 401(k) plans to offer lifetime income. It created a safe harbor for employers that select an insurer according to set criteria, requires plan statements to show the account balance also as an estimated lifetime monthly income, and allows annuity investments to be moved out of the plan if the plan drops the option. Some plans therefore offer an annuity purchase at retirement or an investment option with a built-in income guarantee.

The statement figure follows the same reasoning as this lesson. A withdrawal plan covers the probable years of life at low cost, and an annuity insures against improbably long lives. Anyone who takes the whole balance as a lump sum or rolls it into an IRA has to arrange this protection themselves, through the claiming age for Social Security, an income annuity or a cautious withdrawal rule.

mitnehmen: The guaranteed monthly income per $100,000 for the same age and options is the only figure with which income annuities can be compared; quotes differ between insurers.
Thanks to mortality credits, a lifelong income annuity pays more than a fixed-term plan to 95 at the same interest rate; in the model, about $631 instead of $507 a month per $100,000.
Compared with a Treasury account at 4.5%, the model annuity pays off from about age 85, because it is insurance against a long life and not an investment.
A nonqualified annuity is taxed with the exclusion ratio, so only part of each payment is taxable; an annuity bought in an IRA is fully taxable.

The yardstick for annuitization is the gap in basic needs, not the assets; delaying Social Security is often the cheapest inflation-protected lifetime income, and the non-annuitized part provides flexibility and the inheritance.

begriffe.text: Insurance contract bought with a single payment that pays a lifelong income, starting within a year, without an accumulation phase. The insured risk is that of living longer than your own capital lasts.
Guaranteed annual income of an annuity as a percentage of the premium. It rises with the age at purchase and with interest rates and falls with options such as a period certain or a refund.

The part of an annuity's income that comes from the capital of buyers who die early and is paid to those who live longer. It is the reason why a lifelong annuity can pay more than a fixed-term payout at the same interest rate.

Deferred income annuity bought with money from an IRA or employer plan up to an inflation-adjusted limit. Its income can start as late as age 85, and the amount invested is excluded from the RMD calculation until then.
The risk of living considerably longer than average life expectancy and using up your own capital in the process. It can only be handed over completely with a lifelong payment.
